clue.text: Insubstantial fighting unit in which anger's rising

indicators.note: in a down clue something rising is read from bottom to top, so the phrase runs backwards
'in which' says the following phrase sits inside the unit just named

blocks.note: an arm of the services, such as the infantry, is a fighting unit
anger's means 'of ire', ire being anger

explanation.surface: A military unit is dismissed as flimsy while its members seethe with mounting fury.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s has to be read as 'of', so anger's is a two-word phrase, and in a down clue rising means it reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeriform means having the form of air, gaseous, hence unreal or lacking substance.

clue.text: Is longing to illustrate 2012 London Olympics (finals only)

indicators.note: only the finals means keeping just the closing letter of each word

blocks.note: 2012 is an example of a year, which it illustrates
the last letters of London and Olympics

explanation.surface: Someone pines to depict the London Olympic Games of 2012.
explanation.walkthrough: 2012 is not the definition of anything: it is an instance, which is why the clue says 'illustrate'. The definition is the verb phrase 'Is longing', third person like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to long or pine for something, so 'yearns' equals 'is longing'.

clue.text: $1 to secure firm, could it be?

definitions.text: $1 to secure firm, could it be?

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: a buck is slang for one dollar
firm, as in fixed tight, is fast

explanation.surface: A single dollar being enough to buy a company sounds like a quick profit.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: buying a firm for one dollar would be easy money, which the question mark flags as speculation.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast buck is money made quickly and easily, and acquiring a company for one dollar would be just that kind of quick gain.

clue.text: Warner, Yorkshire banker, put in home for workers

indicators.note: something put in is placed inside the other word

blocks.note: a beep is a warning sound, so the thing that warns
a banker is a river (it has banks); the Esk runs through North Yorkshire to Whitby

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire banker called Warner is installed in a house for employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warner' looks like a surname and 'banker' like a job; one is a warning sound, the other a river, since a river has banks. The Esk flows through North Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: A bee skep is a domed straw hive, the home of the worker bees.

clue.text: Does pig in all right and fine about it?

indicators.note: about means going around, so the outer letters wrap around what comes before

blocks.note: all right is OK and fine is OK: two OKs
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question whether a pig in the pen is healthy and fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like the auxiliary verb starting a question; it is the verb 'does' in the sense of performs, with pig as its subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Oinking is the grunting noise a pig makes, so 'oinks' is what a pig does.

clue.text: Perhaps Castellaneta will fill speaking role vacancy

indicators.note: to fill something is to go inside it, so this name is placed within the next word

blocks.note: Dan Castellaneta, the actor who plays Homer Simpson; 'perhaps' marks his first name as one example
a voice part is a speaking role, as in an animated show

explanation.surface: An American voice actor is about to take on a vacant speaking part.
explanation.walkthrough: Dan Castellaneta voices Homer in The Simpsons, which makes the surface apt; 'perhaps' marks his first name as one example of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Voidance is the state of being void, especially a church benefice left without an incumbent: a vacancy.

clue.text: Sadly not in van M&S make sure I've got it

indicators.note: van means the front, so these letters are dropped from the front of each word
sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters end up in a muddled order

blocks.note: the two letters of the shop's initials, to be taken away
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopper laments that Marks & Spencer (M&S, a British chain store) has not checked the van.
explanation.walkthrough: M and S head the words make and sure, so dropping them from the van leaves AKE URE, which is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Eureka, Greek for 'I have found it', is the cry of sudden discovery, the same as 'I've got it'.

clue.text: Did jobs of note ahead of me joining the crossword team

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the plural past tense, as in 'jobs were (done)'

blocks.note: setters often refer to themselves as 'we'
in sol-fa, re is the note just before mi (also written me)

explanation.surface: Someone describes notable work done before they joined the setters' team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ahead of me' is not about seniority: it is the sol-fa scale, where re comes ahead of me (mi). RE then joins WE.
explanation.definitionFit: Were is the plural past form of 'be', the verb that pairs with a plural subject like jobs, as 'did' does.

clue.text: Output from giant iron pipe twisted from pump's core

indicators.note: twisted round means turned the other way, so the pipe is read backwards
the core of a word is its middle, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
a fife is a small flute, a pipe
of can mean from, as in 'born of'
the two middle letters of pump

explanation.surface: A giant's iron pipe gets bent out of shape by a pump.
explanation.walkthrough: FE, then FIFE reversed, then OF, then the middle of pump: the giant's chant in Jack and the Beanstalk.
explanation.definitionFit: Fee-fi-fo-fum is the chant the giant utters in Jack and the Beanstalk, so it is a giant's spoken output.

clue.text: Prim gentleman interrupts retiring loggers

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into, so this title sits inside the other word
retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the whole is read in the reverse direction

blocks.note: prim and staid both mean sedate and proper
sir is the form of address for a gentleman

explanation.surface: A prissy gentleman barges in on lumberjacks as they head off to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Loggers suggests timber workers, but here they are people who log events. The insertion happens first, and then the whole is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Diarists keep a daily written record, which is what logging means in the sense of keeping a log.

clue.text: Find one gradually filtering through vital organ

indicators.note: gradually means step by step, so every other letter is taken
filtering through means passing into, so these letters go inside the word that follows

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of find one
vital and key both mean essential

explanation.surface: A medical description of a substance slowly seeping through an essential body part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vital organ' reads as one phrase, but vital is the wordplay and organ alone is the definition. The kidney filters blood, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: The kidney is one of the body's organs, so it is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Spooner's glory in bank lunch?

indicators.note: William Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds here trade places

blocks.note: boast in an old sense means glory; its opening sound swaps with the next word's
a reef is a bank of rock or sand in the sea; its opening sound swaps with the previous word's

explanation.surface: A reverend's glory might be a lunch at the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: BOAST REEF has its first sounds swapped. The question mark admits that roast beef is only one example of a lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Roast beef is a classic British Sunday lunch, an example of a midday meal.

clue.text: "Kept in cask" won't apply to bottle

indicators.note: to bottle is to hold inside a container, so the words hold the answer within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A label saying 'kept in the barrel' doesn't apply to bottled beer.
explanation.walkthrough: The beer surface makes 'bottle' look like a vessel, but it is the verb that holds the answer inside 'won't apply'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer on tap is drawn straight from a cask or keg rather than served in bottles.

clue.text: "Inflamed eyeball" defining child's complaint

indicators.note: defining, read as de-fining, sets bounds around something, so one piece wraps around the other
something inflamed is stirred up and disturbed, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
ch is the standard abbreviation for child

explanation.surface: A sore eye is diagnosed as the illness a small child has.
explanation.walkthrough: CH goes inside the eyeball's letters and the whole is mixed up. 'Child's complaint' looks like the definition, but child is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellyache is a stomach pain, an ailment, and in slang also a moan, both senses of complaint.

clue.text: Alphameric alphabets sweeping the country

indicators.note: sweeping across words means running through them, so the answer is carried within

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Alphanumeric writing systems are taking a nation by storm.
explanation.walkthrough: Alphameric means made of letters and numbers; the answer spans its end and the first letter of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: America is commonly used as the name of a country, the United States.

clue.text: Ethiopian princess, having run over to king, spoke?

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the princess and the run are read backwards

blocks.note: Aida is the Ethiopian princess in Verdi's opera
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run
taken as written
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: An Ethiopian princess dashes across to the king: did she speak?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoke' looks like the past tense of speak, but it is the wheel part; the question mark warns that the answer is defined by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoke radiates from a wheel's hub, so in the cryptic sense it is something that radiates.

clue.text: Items primarily erased by deadline, possibly

definitions.text: Items primarily erased by deadline, possibly

indicators.note: erased means rubbed out, so this letter is taken away
possibly tells us the letters could form another arrangement

blocks.note: the first letter of items, the one to be erased
taken as written

explanation.surface: Things to be deleted before the deadline, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the I out of deadline and rearrange. The whole clue also describes the answer: delenda are items to be erased, perhaps by a deadline.
explanation.definitionFit: Delenda is Latin for things to be deleted or destroyed, so items to be erased.

clue.text: In a burst blows away last of pretty good times

indicators.note: a burst breaks things apart, so the letters scatter and regroup
blowing away the final letter means the new letters take its place at the end

blocks.note: decent means reasonably good
taken as written

explanation.surface: In a sudden explosion the final remnant of good times disappears.
explanation.walkthrough: The T at the end of DECENT is replaced by IN A rearranged. 'Pretty good times' reads as one phrase, but times alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Decennia is the plural of decennium, a period of ten years, so it names spans of time.

clue.text: Removing this for giving female thrills?

definitions.text: Removing this for giving female thrills?

indicators.note: thrills send a shiver through, so the letters are shaken into a new order
in this compound anagram, removing names letters taken out of the mixture, as well as being the word removed

blocks.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder
these letters are subtracted from the fodder

explanation.surface: A cheeky question: would taking this off give a woman a thrill?
explanation.walkthrough: A compound anagram: the letters of 'for giving female' rearrange into 'removing' plus the answer. The whole clue also hints at its striptease meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A fig leaf is the modest covering on nude statues; taking it off would be a striptease thrill.

clue.text: Who'd mock the first of your greetings?

definitions.note: plural in the clue, while the answer is one greeting; the question mark covers it

indicators.note: a mock version is a fake imitation, so the letters are reworked
the first of a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
the first letter of your

explanation.surface: A wounded question: who would make fun of your friendly hellos?
explanation.definitionFit: Howdy is an informal greeting, a contraction of 'how do you do', common in the American West.

clue.text: Choose not to work with solicitor

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
a tout solicits custom; the clue's solicitor is not a lawyer

explanation.surface: Someone declines to work alongside a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: Solicitor suggests the British lawyer, but here it is one who solicits trade, a tout.
explanation.definitionFit: To opt out is to choose not to take part, matching the infinitive-taking verb phrase.

clue.text: Immerse delicate clothes twinkling about management skills

indicators.note: the word sits next to about, which read as 'turned about' means going backwards
to clothe something is to cover it, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: to dip is to immerse briefly
lacy means delicate, like lace
a twinkling is a moment, mo for short

explanation.surface: Laundry instructions: soak the delicate garments that are glittering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delicate clothes' reads as laundry, but clothes is a verb, and a twinkling is a moment, here turned about.
explanation.definitionFit: Diplomacy is skill in managing people and negotiations tactfully.

clue.text: Posh kept record after cancellation of Glastonbury?

indicators.note: cancellation means scrapping, so the named piece is taken away

blocks.note: to monitor is to keep a record of
Glastonbury Tor is the famous hill in Somerset

explanation.surface: A well-off person kept a diary after the Glastonbury music festival was called off.
explanation.walkthrough: Glastonbury suggests the festival, but it is the Tor, the hill above the town, that is cancelled from MONITORED.
explanation.definitionFit: Monied (moneyed) means wealthy, and posh is informal for upper-class or rich.

clue.text: Pharmacist stitches these drinkers up

indicators.note: stitches hold material within them, so the answer is held inside the word
in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters inside pharmacist

explanation.surface: A chemist sews up a group of heavy drinkers, perhaps after a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: CAMRA, the Campaign for Real Ale, is a British organisation of beer enthusiasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Campaign for Real Ale are drinkers who champion traditional British beer.

clue.text: Inverted power packs zip a Canadian's home

indicators.note: inverted means turned upside down, so the unit is read backwards
to pack something is to stuff it in, so one piece goes between the others

blocks.note: zip is nothing, O
the watt is the unit of power
taken as written

explanation.surface: Upside-down electricity is stuffed into a Canadian's house.
explanation.definitionFit: Ottawa is Canada's capital city, so it is the home of Canadians' government, a national home.

clue.text: Knowledge new driver acquires in employment

blocks.note: L is the plate on a learner driver's car in the UK
someone in employment is earning

explanation.surface: A newly qualified driver picks up know-how on the job.
explanation.definitionFit: Learning is acquired knowledge, as in a person of great learning.

clue.text: Impossible to get to four resorts singly

indicators.note: read as re-sorts, sorting again puts the letters in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
singly, one at a time, means each

explanation.surface: Four holiday spots, taken one by one, can't be visited.
explanation.walkthrough: Resorts looks like holiday places; read as re-sorts it mixes four and to.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of reach means beyond arm's length or unattainable, so not possible to get to.

clue.text: Chief problem's back to front

indicators.note: the back letter moves to the front of the word

blocks.note: a mire is a difficulty or problem

explanation.surface: The main trouble is that it is the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back to front' suggests a full reversal, which would give ERIM; only the last letter moves.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim ruler or commander, a chief.
